1023.title: St Patrick (17 March)
1023.hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me
1023.howItsDone: Catholic and Anglican churches, and some others, keep St Patrick's feast with services and prayers, and the Breastplate is sung as a hymn or said as a morning prayer in some churches; in Ireland it is also a national holiday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three forties, each with a far side, and your line was forty is enough.

Green rivers, marching bands, a parade down the main street of cities nowhere near Ireland. That's one St Patrick's day. There's a quieter one, and it starts with a short piece of writing by the man himself. In it he doesn't sound like a hero. He sounds embarrassed. He says he was not a learned man, that he writes clumsily, that as a young man he didn't really know God. Then he tells how he was stolen from home, carried across the sea and made a slave in a strange country. The parade remembers a national saint. His own words remember a kidnapped boy.
screen: `A SHORT ACCOUNT BY THE MAN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Patrick's own account is called his Confession. He grew up in Britain, in a Christian family, but says he paid its faith little attention. Raiders took him captive to Ireland, where he was set to watch flocks on the hillsides. And there, alone, cold and hungry, he began to pray, he says, day and night, in snow and frost and rain. After years of this, a voice in his sleep told him a ship was ready. He ran, found the ship, and got home. That should be the end. Instead he dreams of a man bringing letters, one headed the voice of the Irish, calling him, as he tells it, to come and walk among them again. And he goes back, to the country of his slavery, to spend his life there. Tradition gives Patrick a hymn called the Breastplate, a prayer you put on like armor before going out. Whether he wrote it is uncertain; it isn't in his Confession. But it sounds like someone who knows what it is to be alone in a hostile place. In one English version: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Every direction covered; nowhere left empty. Some readers hear in it the shepherd boy on the hillside, finding out he was never alone. The shamrock and the snakes come later, from legend. The Confession is where the man himself speaks.
screen: `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH CALLS HIM BACK.`

segments.voice: Notice each direction of the Breastplate in turn: what's in front of you, behind, the ground beneath, the sky or ceiling above, your right, your left. If you pray, say the lines as you go, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me; if not, notice you're held on every side, by the floor, the air, the room, and rest in the middle of it.
St Patrick. A boy taken as a slave to Ireland who escaped, then chose to go back, and whose name is tied to a prayer that fills every direction with Christ.
Your line: christ beside me. Before, behind, above, below. Day one thousand twenty-three, done.

1024.title: St Joseph (19 March)
1024.hook: the quiet carpenter, patron of workers and fathers
1024.howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of St Joseph in March, and in parts of Italy and among Italian-American families, St Joseph's tables of food are set out and shared with the poor; Anglicans and some Lutherans also keep his day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Patrick, a kidnapped boy who went back, and your line was christ beside me.

Go through the Gospels looking for a single sentence spoken by Joseph, the husband of Mary. You'll come up empty. He has dreams. He gets up in the night. He takes a pregnant fiancée into his home, walks a family to Egypt and back, searches the city for a missing twelve-year-old. The text never once records him saying a word. Mary speaks. Simeon speaks. Angels speak. Joseph acts. After the stories of Jesus's childhood, he never appears in a scene again. Churches still give him a feast day. Today, St Joseph.
screen: `HE DREAMS. HE GETS UP. HE GOES.`

segments.voice: Matthew's story of Joseph opens at a painful moment. Mary, the woman he's promised to, is pregnant, and not by him. The King James Bible says: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." Before any angel, his first instinct is to spare her shame, quietly. Then an angel comes in a dream and tells him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife. All Matthew gives of his response is this: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife." No speech. No argument. He wakes up and does it. The pattern repeats. Another dream: take the child and flee. Matthew says he arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt. Up in the dark, packing, gone. Later, when the danger is over, home again. Then his work. In his home town, people later ask about Jesus, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" The Greek word behind carpenter means a builder or craftsman, someone who works with his hands. Mark calls Jesus himself the carpenter, so tradition pictures him learning the trade from this quiet man. That's why Catholics in particular honor Joseph as patron of workers, fathers and families. Some Orthodox and Protestant Christians honor him too, as the righteous man who sheltered the holy family. The picture is of faith that shows up mostly as getting up and doing the next thing.
screen: `A JUST MAN, MINDED TO SPARE HER SHAME.`
`RAISED FROM SLEEP, HE DID AS BIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who looked after you and mostly showed up rather than talked: your father, if that's a good place to go, or a grandfather, an uncle, a coach, a neighbor who once fixed your bike and asked nothing for it. Let one thing they did come back clearly, and if you pray, thank God for them by name; if not, hold the memory with gratitude.
St Joseph. The husband of Mary and the carpenter of Nazareth, who in the Gospels never speaks, and keeps getting up to do what he was asked.

1025.title: The Annunciation (25 March)
1025.hook: nine months before Christmas; once the start of the new year in England
1025.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the Annunciation as a major feast in spring, and in some places the Angelus is still rung or prayed at morning, noon and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Joseph, who never says a word in the Gospels and keeps getting up to act. Your line was the quiet one.

Count forward nine months from today and you land on Christmas. The feast of the angel's visit to Mary is kept in spring, a pregnancy's length before the birth. And for a long stretch of English history, this was also the day the year itself turned over. Not midwinter. Late March. Dates on letters and legal papers changed their year here, on the feast English people called Lady Day. A country turned its calendar on a conversation in Nazareth. Today, the Annunciation.

Luke opens the scene with a time stamp of his own: "And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth." The sixth month of her cousin Elizabeth's pregnancy. The story itself is already counting months. Gabriel greets her: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says she was troubled, and wondered what kind of greeting this was. Then the message: she will conceive and bear a son, and call his name Jesus. She asks how, since she has no husband. The angel answers, and she replies: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Advent already stayed with that yes. Today the feast asks something else of it: when. Christian tradition holds that this is the moment God took flesh, not at the manger but here, hidden, months before anyone could see. Some readers see that thinking behind keeping the feast nine months before Christmas, and behind once starting the year here. The new thing had begun, even if it didn't show. For a long time, church bells marked the moment every day too. The Angelus, rung in some Catholic and Anglican places morning, noon and evening, is a short prayer that walks back through this scene: the angel's message, Mary's answer, and the Word made flesh. Tradition pictures farmers stopping in the fields at the bell, noon in the middle of a working day, set aside to remember Mary's yes.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Practice a noon pause now, so it's ready when midday comes: stop your hands, look up, and take three slow breaths. If you pray, say Mary's answer, be it unto me according to thy word; if you don't, ask yourself what you're saying yes to today, and sit in the quiet that follows.
The Annunciation. The angel's announcement to Mary, kept as a feast nine months before Christmas, the hidden start of the Christmas story.
Your line: nine months to go. Begun, though it doesn't show yet. That's day one thousand twenty-five.

1026.title: Mothering Sunday
1026.hook: in Britain and Ireland, mid-Lent: a day to visit the mother church and your mother
1026.howItsDone: In Britain and Ireland, Mothering Sunday falls in the middle of Lent; churches often give children flowers to hand to their mothers, and families send cards, visit or share a meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation, kept nine months before Christmas, and your line was nine months to go.

A young woman walks a country lane early on a Sunday in spring, in her one good dress, with wildflowers picked from the hedge. She works as a servant in a big house miles away, and this is one of the few days a year she's let go home. She'll go to the church where she was baptized, then to her mother's door. That's the scene tradition paints of this day in Britain and Ireland, in the middle of Lent, when the fast eased for one Sunday and people went back to where they came from. Today it's mostly cards and flowers. Underneath is an older idea of who your mother is.

In the middle of Lent's long weeks, the Western church kept a Sunday with a lighter tone. Its old opening words came from Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her." And in the English prayer book, the letter read that Sunday came from Galatians, where Paul writes: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." Jerusalem as a mother. The church as a mother. So the first mothering, tradition says, was going back to your mother church: the church where you were baptized, or the great church of your area. People who had moved away came home for it, and then, naturally, went home to their actual mothers too. The custom grew warm edges. Servants were given the day. Children picked flowers on the walk. Some families baked a rich fruit cake, allowed in the eased fast. Over time the church side faded for some families and the mother side stayed: cards, flowers and phone calls home. Some confuse it with the American Mother's Day, which began separately; this one grew from a Sunday in the church year. The old custom sets two things side by side: a place that made you, and a person who made you. The answer to both was the same: a walk down the lane, flowers from the hedge, and a knock at the door.

In your mind, walk the road home, street by street, to a door where someone mothered you: your mother's, a grandmother's, an aunt's, a neighbor's, a friend's mom who fed you, whichever you can walk up to gladly. Let one kindness from that house come back, a plate set down, a coat buttoned. If you pray, name her before God on the step; if not, simply stand there with her a moment.
Mothering Sunday. A Sunday in the middle of Lent when people in Britain and Ireland went back to their mother church, and then to their mothers.
Your line: go home. Any door you can walk up to gladly. Until tomorrow.

1027.title: Lazarus Saturday
1027.hook: the Orthodox celebrate Lazarus raised, the day before Palm Sunday
1027.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday, with a service that retells John 11 and, in some places, by making palm crosses or special breads for the next day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mothering Sunday: back to the mother church, then to your mother's door. Your line was go home.

A message reaches Jesus from two sisters in Bethany, Mary and Martha. In the King James Bible it's one line: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. And Jesus waits two more days. By the time he reaches Bethany, Lazarus has been in the grave four days. Martha comes out to meet him on the road, later Mary falls at his feet, and each says the same sentence: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Then Jesus stands before a cave with a stone across it and asks for the stone to be rolled away. Martha, practical to the end, warns him about the smell. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, Orthodox Christians tell this whole story again.

John tells this one slowly, and three short lines carry it. The first is two words long: "Jesus wept." He stands with the sisters at the grave, and he weeps. John doesn't skip the grief to hurry on to the miracle, and neither does Jesus. The second is a shout. In the King James: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still bound hand and foot in grave clothes, his face wrapped in a cloth. The third is easy to miss. Jesus turns to the people standing around and says: "Loose him, and let him go." Jesus calls him out; everyone else has to do the unwrapping. Coming back takes a voice, and then a lot of ordinary hands working at knots. Why keep it on this Saturday? Because John sets the two scenes side by side. Right after Bethany, he says, a crowd that had heard about Lazarus took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus on the road into Jerusalem. So Orthodox churches treat this day as a hinge between Lent and Holy Week, a preview of Easter: the one who calls his friend out of a tomb is about to walk toward his own. And John adds a hard detail. After the raising, the chief priests talk about putting Lazarus to death as well. Being called out of the grave didn't make his life safe. It made it visible.

Bring to mind someone who came back from something: an illness, a dark year, a long silence. Picture their face at the worst point and the way it looks now, then think about the hands that helped unwrap them; maybe yours were among them. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if not, simply hold them in mind, glad they came out.
Lazarus Saturday. The day before Palm Sunday, when Orthodox Christians remember Jesus calling his friend out of the tomb at Bethany.
Your line: come out. A voice first, then many hands. That's day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Palm Sunday procession
1028.hook: crowds with palms, in some places olive or willow branches
1028.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday, congregations that keep the procession gather outside, have branches blessed, and process into church singing; in some churches the service then reads the Passion, the story of Jesus's arrest and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus Saturday: a voice at a tomb, and many hands to unwrap the man who walked out. Your line was come out.

A coat lands in the dust of the road. Then another. A man is coming toward Jerusalem on a young donkey, with people ahead of him and behind him, all shouting the same line. Mark says some spread their garments in the way and others cut branches off the trees. John says they were palm branches. On Palm Sunday, churches walk that road again. People gather outside, branches are blessed, and the whole congregation walks in together, carrying whatever grows near them: palms, and in some places olive or willow. Today, the Palm Sunday procession.

Start with the shout, because the crowd didn't make it up. Matthew gives it like this in the King James: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest." That middle line comes straight from Psalm 118, a song of thanks sung by someone arriving at the gates of the house of the Lord. The crowd reaches for words they know by heart and hands them to the man on the donkey. Then the donkey. Matthew says this happened to fulfil a word of the prophet, and in Zechariah it reads: "behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass." A king, but not on a war horse, and not with an army. Lowly. Some readers hear the whole scene as Jesus showing what kind of king he means to be. Now the branches. Only John names palms; Mark just says branches cut off the trees. The churches don't agree on one plant either. Where palms grow, people carry palms; where they don't, they carry what's at hand. The point was never the species. It was a crowd laying something down in the road for someone they hoped in. And here's the turn some churches keep on purpose. The same service that opens with branches and singing goes on to read the whole story of the arrest and the cross. The cheering and the crying out happen in one service, as they happened in one week. The road in leads to Friday.

Hold a branch or a leaf, a sprig from outside, a leaf from a houseplant, or rest one hand open as if you held one, and feel how light it is. If you pray, say the crowd's line, blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; if not, think of what you would lay down for someone you honor.

Your line: blessed is he who comes. A psalm, shouted on the road. Day one thousand twenty-eight, done.

1029.title: Holy Week's middle days
1029.hook: Monday to Wednesday: the fig tree, the temple, the anointing
1029.howItsDone: Some churches hold daily services on the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week, reading the Gospel scenes of these days; some households use them to clean and prepare for Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: branches on the road and a crowd singing a psalm. Your line was blessed is he who comes.

So what happened on the Monday? Between the shouting on the road and the supper on Thursday are a few days that are easy to skip. Mark sets three strange scenes among them. A fig tree covered in leaves and bare of fruit. Tables tipped over in the temple courts, coins rolling on the stones. And a dinner in Bethany where a woman breaks open a jar of perfume and pours it over Jesus's head. Tradition spreads these scenes across the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week: the held breath before everything happens.

First, the tree. Jesus is hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing on it; Mark even adds that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus speaks to it, and the next morning it has withered from the roots. Notice where Mark puts it: the tree comes before the temple scene and the withering after, so each frames the other. Some readers hear in it a warning about any religious life, their own included, that's all leaves and no fruit. Second, the temple. Jesus drives out the people buying and selling and overturns the money tables, quoting the prophets of Israel. In the King James: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." Of all nations. Some readers hear him defending the temple's own calling, in the words of its own scriptures. Third, the jar. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly ointment over his head. Some at the table are indignant: what a waste. Jesus says, let her alone, and then: "She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying." A burial anointing, ahead of time. Right after, Mark says, Judas goes to the chief priests, which is why some places call Wednesday Spy Wednesday. Three quiet scenes. A tree that says nothing. A courtyard cleared. A room full of perfume.
